title: Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner
articleTitle: The Jurisprudence of Innovation: An Exhaustive Analysis of Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner and the Evolving Standards of Funded Research in the United States Tax System
subject: Funded Research Exclusion
summary: Populous Holdings v. Commissioner is a December 2019 U.S. Tax Court order holding that an architectural firm's research under five representative fixed-price contracts was not funded under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), because Populous bore the financial risk of failure and retained substantial rights. The nonprecedential order offers persuasive guidance for design contractors claiming the federal R&D tax credit.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Factual Context and Procedural Posture of the Dispute

In Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, Docket No. 405-17, 2019 WL 13032526 (U.S. Tax Ct. Dec. 6, 2019) (Order served Dec. 9, 2019), the United States Tax Court addressed a foundational question governing the eligibility of architectural, engineering, and technical service contractors for the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 41. The petitioner, Populous Holdings, Inc. ("Populous"), is a prominent architectural design services firm globally recognized for designing complex sports venues, stadiums, and convention centers. For the 2010 and 2011 taxable years, Populous claimed federal research tax credits under I.R.C. § 41 attributable to design and engineering activities performed across more than 100 client contracts and subcontracts under which Populous was the payee. Following an examination, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued a notice of deficiency disallowing $132,539 in research tax credits claimed for the 2011 tax year, alongside a $151,494 general business credit carryforward from the 2010 tax year.

In the ensuing litigation, the Commissioner asserted that Populous's research expenses were for "funded research" excluded under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) because payments under the client contracts were not contingent on the success of the research and, alternatively, because Populous did not retain substantial rights in the research under three of the representative contracts, citing the clients' ownership of the documents Populous produced and, in certain contracts, of the architectural copyrights. On March 15, 2019, Populous and the Commissioner filed cross-motions for summary judgment on the issue of whether Populous was entitled to a credit for qualified research expenses under I.R.C. § 41 for 2011—specifically, whether the research expenses were for funded research excluded from the definition of qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H). To streamline the adjudication of more than 100 separate project agreements, the parties jointly identified five representative contracts (McEnery, Houston Dynamo, University of Arkansas, University of South Florida, and Pico Hall) and agreed that the Tax Court's decision with respect to those five representative contracts would resolve the funded research issue in accordance with the allocation set forth in their stipulation of settled issues.

On December 6, 2019 (served December 9, 2019), U.S. Tax Court Judge Joseph Robert Goeke issued an Order granting Populous's motion for summary judgment and denying the Commissioner's cross-motion. Judge Goeke held that under all five representative contracts, Populous bore the financial risk of the research's failure, and that Populous retained substantial rights in its research under the three contracts the Commissioner challenged on that ground, rendering the work "unfunded" for purposes of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H). Because the deficiency determined in the notice of deficiency differed from the amounts set forth in the parties' stipulation of settled issues, the Order directed the parties to submit a Rule 155 computation to the Court on or before January 15, 2020; according to secondary reports, the Tax Court subsequently entered a stipulated decision on January 16, 2020 reflecting no deficiency in income tax due from, nor overpayment due to, the petitioner for the 2011 taxable year. From a procedural standpoint, tax practitioners must recognize that the Populous Holdings disposition was issued as an unpublished Tax Court Order rather than a division opinion or memorandum opinion; under U.S. Tax Court Rule 50(f), an order is nonprecedential and cannot be cited as binding legal precedent, though it serves as persuasive authority illustrating the Tax Court's analytical methodology for fixed-price design contracts. Moreover, because the IRS hinged its summary judgment posture strictly on the funded research exclusion, the Order did not adjudicate whether the underlying architectural design activities satisfied the substantive four-part test for "qualified research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1).
The Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

Enacted originally in 1981 to incentivize domestic technological innovation, the federal research credit regime established under I.R.C. § 41 provides a nonrefundable tax credit equal to 20 percent of the amount by which a taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year exceed a statutory base amount, or 14 percent under the Alternative Simplified Credit election of I.R.C. § 41(c)(4). Pursuant to I.R.C. § 41(b), eligible QREs comprise "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses". In-house research expenses encompass wages paid or incurred to an employee for performing "qualified services"—specifically defined under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) as engaging in qualified research, directly supervising qualified research, or directly supporting qualified research—as well as amounts paid or incurred for tangible "supplies" used in the conduct of qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C), excluding land, improvements to land, and property subject to depreciation. Contract research expenses under I.R.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) allow a taxpayer to claim 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred to a non-employee third party for the performance of qualified research "on behalf of" the taxpayer, subject to strict risk-allocation and substantial-rights rules under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e). While domestic research and experimental expenditures are separately governed for deduction and capitalization purposes by I.R.C. § 174—which was modified on July 4, 2025, by Public Law 119-21, commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act—research credit eligibility under I.R.C. § 41 remains an independent and substantially stricter statutory inquiry.

To qualify for the credit under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a), the underlying technical activities must satisfy a cumulative four-part statutory test applied separately to each discrete business component. First, under the Section 174 Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), the expenditures must qualify as expenses under I.R.C. § 174, meaning they must be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense intended to discover information that would eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving a product or process. Second, under the Technological in Nature Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the activity must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, requiring that the process of experimentation fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Business Component and Permitted Purpose Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), § 41(d)(2)(B), and § 41(d)(3)(A), the taxpayer must intend to apply the discovered information to develop a new or improved business component (defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business) for a qualified functional purpose—specifically improved function, performance, reliability, or quality—while I.R.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) expressly disqualifies activities relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6), substantially all (defined quantitatively as 80 percent or more) of the research activities applied to the business component must constitute elements of a structured process of experimentation that evaluates one or more technical alternatives to resolve the design, method, or capability uncertainty.

Even where a taxpayer satisfies all four requirements of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), Congress enacted eight categorical exclusions under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4), including exclusions for research after commercial production (§ 41(d)(4)(A)), adaptation of an existing business component (§ 41(d)(4)(B)), duplication of an existing business component (§ 41(d)(4)(C)), surveys, routine data collection, and routine quality control testing (§ 41(d)(4)(D)), foreign research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, or U.S. possessions (§ 41(d)(4)(F)), and research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities (§ 41(d)(4)(G)). For architectural, engineering, and custom manufacturing contractors, the primary statutory hurdle is the Funded Research Exclusion codified at I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), which mandates that qualified research shall not include "any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)".

Because the statute does not define the term "funded," the interpretive rules are established in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), which is explicitly incorporated by reference into the qualified research regulations via Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), to determine the extent to which research is funded, the examining authority and the courts must inspect "all agreements (not only research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons". This regulatory regime institutes a bifurcated inquiry evaluating both the contingency of payment (financial risk) and the retention of substantial rights. Under the first prong (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)), amounts payable under an agreement that are contingent on the success of the research—and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research—are not treated as funding. This provision mirrors the contract research rule at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii), ensuring that a single research expenditure is neither claimed twice (by both client and contractor) nor orphaned when a party genuinely bears the economic risk of failure. Under the second prong (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)), if a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in the research under the terms of the agreement, the research is treated as fully funded and 100 percent disqualified, even if payment was entirely contingent on the success of the research. Furthermore, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) expressly dictates that "incidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research". Conversely, under the partial funding rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3), if a taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research results, but client payments are not contingent on research success (such as under an unconditional time-and-materials contract), the research is treated as funded only "to the extent of the payments (and fair market value of any property) to which the taxpayer becomes entitled by performing the research," applied separately on a project-by-project basis pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(iii).

body.text: The Tax Authority's Challenge and the Court's Final Holding

In Populous Holdings, the Commissioner challenged the taxpayer's claim across both prongs of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). Under the financial risk prong, the IRS contended that payments under all five representative contracts were not contingent on the success of the research. Under the substantial rights prong, the IRS argued in the alternative—if the court held the contingency requirement satisfied—that Populous did not retain substantial rights in three of the five representative contracts (McEnery, Pico Hall, and Houston Dynamo), and it did not challenge substantial rights under the other two. The IRS's argument focused on the clients' ownership of the documents Populous produced: under the McEnery contract, the client owned all design documents, construction documents, and other documents such as studies, manuals, as-built drawings, and technical and other reports, and held sole rights to the architectural copyrights; under the Pico Hall contract, the client owned the architectural copyrights and the construction documents, models, renderings, and other work product, and the contract also prohibited Populous from using or recreating any distinctive original, material exterior features without the client's consent; and under the Houston Dynamo contract, the client owned the project-related documents, with Populous retaining rights only to design details that were repetitive in nature, not project specific, and preexisting.

Judge Goeke rejected both of the Commissioner's arguments. Addressing financial risk under Prong One, the Tax Court synthesized the precedent established by the Federal Circuit in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995) and the Eleventh Circuit in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015). Judge Goeke framed the inquiry around who bears the economic cost of the research if the research fails. Noting that courts have considered payment procedures, quality and performance standards, termination clauses, and warranty and default provisions, and having reviewed all relevant contract provisions (including the standards of care and termination provisions), the court emphasized that all five representative contracts were fixed price—three of them (McEnery, Houston Dynamo, and University of Arkansas) also providing a capped reimbursement of certain expenses that did not relate to research—and that Populous was paid for a work product at a fixed price that included the need to perform research. Reasoning that, if its research failed, Populous would be required to incur additional expenses without additional compensation, and noting that all five contracts granted the clients the right to review and approve design documents and to dispute invoices (and that the Houston Dynamo and Pico Hall contracts expressly required Populous to revise documents under certain circumstances at its own expense, while the University of Arkansas contract provided for revisions without expressly stating they were at Populous's expense), Judge Goeke concluded that payments were contingent on the research's success in all five contracts and that Populous bore the financial risk of the research's failure.

Addressing substantial rights under Prong Two, Judge Goeke applied the Federal Circuit's framework in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), under which the right to use the research without paying the client is a substantial retained right, that right need not be exclusive, and incidental benefits such as increased knowledge or experience do not constitute substantial rights in the research. Judge Goeke reasoned that, although the Commissioner's argument focused on the clients' ownership of the documents Populous produced, ownership of documents does not dictate the right to use technology-related research results or mean that the clients had an exclusive right to Populous's research. Because Populous retained copies of the documents for its use and none of the three challenged contracts contained a provision prohibiting Populous from using the research it performed or requiring it to pay the client for use of the research, the Tax Court held that Populous retained substantial rights. Having satisfied both regulatory prongs across all five representative agreements, Populous was granted summary judgment on the funded research issue.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

Although Populous prevailed on summary judgment in its December 2019 nonprecedential Order, a comprehensive legal and technical evaluation of the ruling—particularly when analyzed alongside subsequent U.S. appellate and Tax Court jurisprudence—reveals four critical contractual, legal, and evidentiary vulnerabilities—some contested in, and others left unresolved by, Populous Holdings—that have subsequently caused catastrophic taxpayer disqualifications in binding federal decisions.
Contractual Silence on Research and the Fixed-Price Contingency Fallacy

The primary contractual feature at issue in Populous Holdings was the complete absence of express contractual terms requiring the performance of research or tying client payment to the technical success of an experimental process. As Judge Goeke explicitly acknowledged in his Order, "None of the contracts expressly requires research; thus, none of the contracts expressly states that petitioner is being paid for research. Petitioner is paid for a work product at a fixed price. The work product included the need to perform research." To bridge this contractual silence, Judge Goeke relied in part on the generalization that "in general, fixed priced contracts have been considered unfunded research, qualifying the contractor for the credit".

In the years following December 2019, this exact contractual vulnerability—relying on a standard commercial fixed-price fee structure without express research-contingency language—has been systematically dismantled by the IRS and the federal courts of appeals. In Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 7805-16 (T.C. Nov. 19, 2020) (order granting summary judgment to the Commissioner), aff'd, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. May 6, 2024) ("MBJ"), a structural engineering firm creating construction documents for building projects under fixed-price contracts cited Judge Goeke's Populous Holdings Order to argue that its fixed-price contracts containing client inspection and quality assurance clauses were unfunded. The Tax Court ruled for the Commissioner on summary judgment, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, noting that it was a nonprecedential order under Tax Court Rule 50(f), declined to follow Populous Holdings and ruled that the taxpayer's research was 100 percent funded because "none of the contracts expressly or by clear implication make payment contingent on the success of MBJ's research".

Similarly, in United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602, 618–20 (5th Cir. 2023), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed a lower court ruling and held a design-build construction contractor's fixed-price contract to be funded research. Together, the Fifth and Eighth Circuits, alongside the Tax Court in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (issued June 16, 2026) and IRS Chief Counsel in Field Attorney Advice LAFA 20223401F (Aug. 26, 2022), exposed two fatal analytical flaws in relying upon fixed-price fee structures alone. First, taxpayers improperly conflate "contracts for products or services" with payments contingent on successful research; merely delivering construction blueprints or engineering drawings for a lump sum does not establish that the customer conditioned payment on resolving a technological uncertainty. Second, the appellate courts rejected the proposition that fixed-price contracts are inherently risky and therefore per se unfunded. Every fixed-price commercial contract carries the general economic risk of investing labor and resources without a commitment that the price will cover all costs if hours are underestimated. However, general business risk of cost overruns is legally distinct from financial risk contingent on the technical success of the research itself under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Consequently, tax advisors who rely on Populous Holdings for the proposition that a stipulated-sum or fixed-price architectural or engineering contract automatically passes the financial risk prong expose their clients to summary disallowance under binding appellate precedent.
Standard of Care Clauses Versus Objective Technical Performance Benchmarks

Closely linked to the fixed-price fallacy is a second contractual failure inherent in standard architectural and engineering agreements, such as unmodified American Institute of Architects (AIA) or Engineers Joint Contract Documents Committee (EJCDC) templates: the reliance on a professional "standard of care" covenant coupled with routine phase approvals, rather than binding technical performance warranties and clawback or refund remedies. In Populous Holdings, Judge Goeke reviewed the contracts' standards of care, staged document review provisions, invoice dispute rights, and termination clauses, concluding that they collectively placed financial risk on the architect. However, in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330, 1340–43 (11th Cir. 2015), Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (8th Cir. 2024), Smith v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-50), and LAFA 20223401F, the federal courts and the IRS established a strict dichotomy between "proper performance" and "successful performance".

When an architect or engineer contracts to deliver design documents prepared with ordinary professional skill and care, in compliance with applicable municipal building codes, and free from professional negligence, the contractor's right to payment is conditioned merely on professional diligence and code compliance—which constitutes "proper performance". As the Eleventh Circuit held in Geosyntec and the Eighth Circuit reaffirmed in MBJ, contracting to perform pursuant to a general professional standard of care "does not mandate success" of the underlying research. Furthermore, staged progress payments approved after client review of schematic designs or construction documents merely confirm that the contractor completed the scheduled scope of services, rather than verifying that an uncertain technological hypothesis succeeded.

By contrast, the judicial gold standard for "successful performance" (unfunded research) remains Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868, 870–74 (Fed. Cir. 1995), where the taxpayer's fixed-price contract with the U.S. Air Force to develop the T-46A aircraft contained over 1,000 pages of binding technical specifications. Crucially, in Fairchild, the Air Force could reject any line item that failed to meet quantitative physical performance metrics, withhold payment, or require Fairchild to refund progress advances already received if the research failed to satisfy formal acceptance testing. Similarly, in the procedural summary judgment order in System Technologies (Docket No. 12211-21), the Tax Court denied the IRS partial summary judgment only because applicable state commercial law (Indiana law) provided an overarching statutory refund remedy if the company failed to deliver the promised functioning product. Where design contracts lack express technical performance barometers, formal non-conformance rejection criteria, and a legal obligation to forfeit or refund prior progress payments upon technical failure, courts applying binding appellate precedent consistently rule that payment is not contingent on research success.
Intellectual Property Assignments, Copyright Transfers, and Substantial Rights Vulnerabilities

The third core area of dispute in Populous Holdings centered on intellectual property ownership clauses that the Commissioner argued disqualified three of the five representative contracts under the "substantial rights" requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2). In those three agreements, the clients owned the documents Populous produced—under the McEnery contract, all design documents, construction documents, and other documents such as studies, manuals, as-built drawings, and technical and other reports; under the Pico Hall contract, the construction documents, models, renderings, and other work product; and under the Houston Dynamo contract, the project-related documents, with Populous retaining rights only to design details that were repetitive in nature, not project specific, and preexisting. Furthermore, in two of those contracts (McEnery and Pico Hall), the client held the architectural copyrights, and the Pico Hall contract also prohibited Populous from using or recreating any distinctive original, material exterior features without the client's consent.

While Judge Goeke ultimately ruled in favor of Populous by applying Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000)—holding that ownership of the documents did not dictate the right to use technology-related research results, and that no provision in the contracts prohibited Populous from using the research it performed or required it to pay the client for use of the research—this contractual posture exposes service providers to three acute legal hazards. First, in commercial procurement practice, client legal departments rarely limit intellectual property transfer clauses to physical drawings and exterior aesthetic features; standard corporate master services agreements (MSAs) routinely define "Work Product" or "Foreground IP" to encompass all inventions, discoveries, technical data, processes, methodologies, formulas, calculations, software scripts, and know-how conceived or reduced to practice during the engagement, vesting exclusive ownership in the client. When a contract transfers ownership of the underlying technical methods or prohibits their disclosure and reuse under a blanket confidentiality or work-for-hire clause, the contractor retains zero substantial rights under Lockheed Martin and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2).

Second, under Lockheed Martin and the substantial-rights analysis applied by Judge Goeke in Populous, if a contract requires the researcher to obtain the client's prior permission or pay a royalty or fee before applying a technical solution developed on the project to a subsequent client's project, substantial rights are destroyed. In Populous, the prior-consent restriction appeared only in the Pico Hall contract and applied to "distinctive original, material exterior features," which the Order equated with use of the client's copyright; the Order did not address whether such features fall within the § 41(d)(3)(B) exclusion. Had that prior-consent restriction extended to structural, mechanical, or parametric design assemblies, the substantial-rights outcome for those contracts could have been different, although the Order did not address that scenario. Third, when a contract is silent on the contractor's right to reuse underlying research results while explicitly vesting all documents and copyrights in the client, the IRS routinely argues—as detailed in LAFA 20223401F—that all the contractor retains is general professional experience and generic skill enhancement, which Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) explicitly excludes as mere "incidental benefits" incapable of constituting substantial rights.
Unlitigated Substantive and Evidentiary Deficiencies Under the Four-Part Test and Section 6001

A vital strategic imperative for tax counsel is recognizing that surviving the threshold funded research exclusion in Populous Holdings does not establish substantive entitlement to the R&D tax credit. Because the IRS in Populous litigated the cross-motions for summary judgment solely on I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), and the Order, after granting Populous's motion, merely directed the parties to submit a Rule 155 computation, the Tax Court never adjudicated whether Populous's architectural activities satisfied the four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) or the substantiation mandates of I.R.C. § 6001. In subsequent Tax Court and appellate decisions involving architectural, engineering, and design-build taxpayers—most notably Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Dec. 23, 2024), Harper v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-57 (May 10, 2023), Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84 (July 6, 2023)—the IRS litigated substantive four-part-test issues; it defeated the taxpayers in Phoenix Design Group, Little Sandy Coal, and Betz (whereas in Harper the Tax Court denied the IRS's motion for summary judgment on the business component issue), and these cases illustrate four pervasive evidentiary failures.

First, architectural and engineering firms frequently fail to isolate discrete qualifying business components and fail to maintain records necessary to execute the "shrinking-back rule" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Firms routinely define an entire building, stadium, or multi-discipline mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) project as a single macro business component. While the Tax Court in Harper v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-57 confirmed that a construction design can constitute a valid business component in principle, the Tax Court in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 disallowed 100 percent of the consulting engineering firm's trial projects and imposed stipulated accuracy-related penalties because the firm failed to prove that the overall building projects satisfied the four-part test and lacked segregated technical and time-tracking records allowing the court to shrink the claim back to a specific experimental subsystem.

Second, design taxpayers consistently fail to separate genuine technological uncertainty from aesthetic design preferences and routine code compliance under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), § 41(d)(3)(B), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3). In architectural engagements, substantial labor is devoted to spatial configuration, visual appearance, sightlines, and exterior or interior styling—activities categorically barred by the style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(d)(3)(B). Concurrently, consulting engineers spend thousands of hours performing standard load calculations, sizing ductwork, selecting commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) equipment, and verifying compliance with municipal building and energy codes. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3), technical uncertainty does not exist if the capability, method, or appropriate design is readily discernible to a skilled professional applying standard engineering practices and published code tables; only when a project constraint forces an assembly outside tested parameters—such as an unprecedented long-span cantilever or a custom acoustic and hygrothermal facade assembly—does qualifying technological uncertainty arise.

Third, service firms regularly fail to substantiate a structured process of experimentation and fail the quantitative "substantially all" (80 percent) threshold of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6). Taxpayers frequently assert that utilizing Building Information Modeling (BIM), Computer-Aided Design (CAD), or energy simulation software on every job inherently constitutes a process of experimentation. In Phoenix Design Group and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the courts held that running standard validation calculations, performing routine quality control testing, or engaging in unstructured trial-and-error without formulating a scientific hypothesis and systematically evaluating technical alternatives fails I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). Moreover, under the Seventh Circuit's decision in Little Sandy Coal, if a taxpayer cannot quantitatively prove that at least 80 percent of the activities applied to the defined business component (properly accounting for direct supervision and direct support activities in the numerator) constituted elements of a process of experimentation, the entire business component is disqualified.

Fourth, architectural and engineering claims frequently collapse under I.R.C. § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2 due to contemporaneous time-tracking and expense allocation failures. Because design firms typically structure project accounting around broad AIA billing phases (Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Documents, Bidding, and Construction Administration) rather than discrete research tasks, claims routinely sweep in excluded hours spent drafting routine construction documents, obtaining municipal permits, performing code compliance reviews, and utilizing unscreened offshore production support—the latter of which is strictly barred by the foreign research exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(F). When firms lack contemporaneous time records linking employee hours to specific experimental sub-components and instead rely on retrospective "departmental approach" percentage estimates, the Tax Court routinely disallows the claimed wage QREs in their entirety.

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement implicated in Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner and subsequent U.S. federal R&D tax credit jurisprudence against the specific contractual or evidentiary failures challenged by the IRS and the governing judicial standard of proof.

In Populous: Fixed-price contracts contained no express requirement to conduct "research" and did not explicitly state that payment was conditioned on research success. In MBJ, Grigsby, & Smith: Relying on fixed-price terms alone as per se unfunded; conflating general economic risk of labor cost overruns with payment conditioned on technical research success.

Holistic Risk & Express Contingency Standard: While Judge Goeke in Populous inferred risk from fixed-price terms, invoice dispute rights, and rework obligations, binding appellate precedent (Fairchild Indus., 71 F.3d 868; Geosyntec, 776 F.3d 1330; Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602; MBJ, 100 F.4th 986) requires that contracts expressly or by clear implication make payment (and the right to retain progress payments) contingent on the technical success of the research, rather than mere delivery of a work product.
Performance Standard vs. Research Acceptance & Refund Remedies I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)

In Populous: Contracts utilized architectural "standard of care" clauses and staged client design document approvals rather than formal research acceptance testing. In Geosyntec, MBJ, & LAFA 20223401F: Promising only to perform with ordinary professional skill and care in compliance with building codes, with no obligation to refund prior progress payments if a technical design fails.

"Successful Performance" vs. "Proper Performance" Standard: Under Fairchild, Geosyntec, and MBJ, adhering to a professional standard of care and building codes constitutes "proper performance," not "successful performance." To prove unfunded status under strict appellate scrutiny, the taxpayer must demonstrate detailed technical specifications, formal client rejection rights for non-conforming technical performance, and a contractual or state-law obligation to cure at its own expense or refund payments received if technical benchmarks fail (Fairchild; System Technologies).
Retention of Substantial Rights in Research I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3)

In Populous: In three of five sample contracts, clients owned the project documents (depending on the contract, design and construction documents, models, renderings, studies, and technical reports); in two of those three (McEnery and Pico Hall), clients held the architectural copyrights, and the Pico Hall contract also barred Populous from using or recreating distinctive original, material exterior features without consent. In LAFA 20223401F: Broad work-for-hire IP clauses transferring underlying technical know-how or leaving the contractor with only generic experience.

Uncompensated & Unrestricted Reuse Standard (Lockheed Martin): Under Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000) and Populous, the taxpayer must show from the contract text that it retained the right to use the research without paying the client—a substantial retained right that need not be exclusive—meaning that no provision prohibits it from using the research it performed or requires it to pay the client for such use; under Populous, client ownership of the documents does not by itself dictate the right to use technology-related research results. Mere "incidental benefits" (increased experience) fail under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2).
Business Component & Shrinking-Back Rule I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii); I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(A)–(B); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)

Unlitigated in Populous (Fatal in Phoenix Design Group): Defining an entire building, stadium, or multi-discipline MEP project as a single macro business component without isolating the specific experimental sub-assemblies or maintaining sub-component accounting records.

Discrete Component & Sub-Component Substantiation Standard: Under Harper v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-57 and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, the taxpayer must identify a specific product, process, technique, or invention intended for functional improvement. If the overall building design includes routine elements, the taxpayer must apply the shrinking-back rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)) to the discrete uncertain subsystem and prove both the four-part test and segregated QREs at that sub-component level.
Technological Uncertainty vs. Aesthetic & Routine Design I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A); I.R.C. § 41(d)(3)(B); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)

Unlitigated in Populous (Fatal in Phoenix Design Group & Betz): Claiming architectural styling, sightline geometry, aesthetic facade appearance (§ 41(d)(3)(B)), or routine engineering load calculations and municipal building code compliance as technical uncertainty.

Objective Engineering Uncertainty Standard: The taxpayer must prove through contemporaneous technical records that as of the outset of the project, information available to the taxpayer did not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design to achieve a functional, performance, reliability, or quality metric (§ 41(d)(3)(A)), and that resolving the issue required going beyond standard engineering tables, building codes, and aesthetic preferences.
Process of Experimentation & "Substantially All" (80%) Rule I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)

Unlitigated in Populous (Fatal in Little Sandy Coal & Phoenix Design Group): Treating standard BIM/CAD modeling, single-pass validation simulations, or unstructured trial-and-error as experimentation; failing to prove that 80%+ of component activities were experimental.

Scientific Method & 80% Quantitative Standard: Under Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023) and Phoenix Design Group, the taxpayer must document a structured process of formulating technical hypotheses, modeling/simulating or testing multiple design alternatives, and analyzing results—and must prove with quantitative time/cost records that at least 80% ("substantially all") of the activities on the business component (including direct supervision/support) constituted elements of that experimental process.
QRE Quantification & Contemporaneous Substantiation I.R.C. § 41(b)(2); I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(F); I.R.C. § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2

Unlitigated in Populous (Fatal in Phoenix Design Group & Machise): Using retrospective oral estimates across broad AIA billing phases; sweeping in construction document drafting, permitting, code compliance, and foreign/offshore production support.

Strict Nexus & Contemporaneous Recordkeeping Standard: Under I.R.C. § 6001 and Phoenix Design Group, the taxpayer bears the burden of establishing a direct nexus between claimed wages/supplies/contract costs and qualified services on specific business components via contemporaneous time-tracking by phase and task, strictly screening out routine production drafting, permitting, indirect administration, and foreign activities under § 41(d)(4)(F).

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how taxpayers and tax counsel can proactively structure complex technical engagements to overcome both the contractual funding challenges litigated in Populous Holdings (and tightened by the appellate courts in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Grigsby, and Geosyntec) and the substantive four-part test failures identified in Phoenix Design Group and Little Sandy Coal, the following two industry case studies provide a step-by-step remedial blueprint.
Case Study 1: Structural and Facade Engineering for a Long-Span Retractable Stadium Roof and High-Performance Thermal Envelope
Baseline Project Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Apex Architectural & Structural Design, Inc. ("Apex"), a United States architectural and structural engineering firm, is engaged by a municipal sports authority ("Owner") to design a 65,000-seat multi-purpose stadium located in a high-seismic, extreme-winter climate zone. The project presents two genuinely uncertain engineering challenges: first, designing an asymmetrical, 720-foot clear-span kinetic retractable roof truss capable of operating under uneven snow-drift loads while withstanding seismic acceleration without binding on its mechanized bogie tracks; and second, developing a unitized double-skin ethylene tetrafluoroethylene (ETFE) and photovoltaic glass facade assembly that prevents interior condensation at ambient temperatures while maintaining a Solar Heat Gain Coefficient (SHGC) below and meeting strict acoustic reverberation limits.

In its unamended baseline posture, Apex executes a modified AIA B101-style Master Design Agreement for a stipulated lump-sum fee of $18,500,000, billed monthly based on percentage of completion across five standard architectural phases (Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Documents, Bidding, and Construction Administration). This baseline structure contains four disqualifying pitfalls identified in Populous Holdings, MBJ, and Phoenix Design Group. First, the contract is completely silent regarding research or experimentation, and monthly progress payments become non-refundable upon the Owner's approval of each design phase, with no clawback or refund provision if a technical system fails to achieve performance metrics. Second, Article 2 of the agreement states only that Apex shall perform its services consistent with the ordinary professional skill and care of architects practicing in the same locality and in compliance with state building codes—classic "proper performance" language held disqualifying in Geosyntec and MBJ. Third, Article 7 designates all "Instruments of Service"—defined broadly to include all drawings, BIM models, parametric scripts, analytical calculations, engineering methodologies, and copyrights—as the exclusive property of the Owner, prohibiting Apex from reusing any project materials or technical designs on future projects without the Owner's prior written consent. Fourth, Apex's project accounting tracks all employee hours to a single master job number ("Job #2026-104: Municipal Stadium"), commingling aesthetic bowl seating geometry, VIP suite interior styling, routine plumbing and electrical code compliance, offshore CAD drafting in India, and the kinetic roof and facade engineering into one undifferentiated cost pool.
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring to Establish Unfunded Status Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)

Before executing the agreement—or through a binding bilateral Contract Addendum executed prior to commencing the experimental design phases—tax counsel must restructure the contract across four operational provisions to satisfy both Populous Holdings and the stricter appellate standard of Fairchild Industries, Grigsby, and MBJ. Rather than burying R&D activities inside a generic 18.5 million lump sum, counsel structures a dedicated "Schedule B: Experimental Engineering & Performance-Contingent Design Scope" covering the Kinetic Roof Structural System (2,400,000 fixed fee) and the High-Performance ETFE/PV Acoustic-Thermal Facade Assembly ($1,600,000 fixed fee). Schedule B explicitly recites that achieving the target structural and hygrothermal performance parameters cannot be accomplished through standard building code tables or known engineering practices and requires Apex to undertake systematic engineering research and experimentation.

While retaining the general professional standard of care for routine architectural services, Schedule B incorporates binding quantitative technical specifications analogous to Fairchild, specifically requiring a maximum truss deflection of under combined unbalanced snow load and spectral seismic acceleration without track-bogie lateral binding, alongside zero interior surface condensation at exterior and interior ( relative humidity), SHGC , and a Noise Reduction Coefficient (NRC). Furthermore, the payment and default clauses for Schedule B stipulate that interim milestone advances are provisional deposits only, and that Apex's legal right to earn and retain the fixed fee for each Schedule B subsystem is expressly contingent upon the subsystem passing third-party peer-reviewed finite element analysis (FEA), boundary-layer wind-tunnel testing, and full-scale physical mock-up chamber testing. If either subsystem fails acceptance testing, Apex is contractually obligated to redesign, re-engineer, and re-test the assembly entirely at its own expense without additional compensation; if Apex fails to achieve the quantitative Schedule B benchmarks within the contractual cure period, the Owner holds the express right to reject the Schedule B deliverables and demand a full refund of all prior provisional payments made under Schedule B.

Finally, Article 7 is amended to mirror the exact intellectual property distinction upheld by Judge Goeke in Populous Holdings and the Federal Circuit in Lockheed Martin. The Owner is granted ownership of the physical construction drawings and sole architectural copyright strictly in the distinctive aesthetic exterior appearance of the stadium. Concurrently, Article 7 explicitly provides that notwithstanding the Owner's ownership of the physical Instruments of Service and exterior architectural copyrights, Apex retains perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive ownership and substantial rights in all underlying engineering research results, structural mechanics, parametric algorithms, thermal and acoustic assembly methodologies, and technical know-how developed during the project, together with full archival copies of all technical models and reports, and may freely use, adapt, and exploit all such research results on future projects for any third party without obtaining the Owner's consent and without paying any royalty, license fee, or other compensation to the Owner.
Step 2: Project Governance and Business Component Isolation via the Shrinking-Back Protocol

To prevent a Phoenix Design Group blanket disallowance, Apex's R&D governance committee prohibits claiming the "Municipal Stadium" as a single macro business component. Instead, applying I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(A) and the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), Apex establishes two discrete, standalone business components in its formal project charter: Business Component 104-A (Long-Span Asymmetrical Seismic-Isolated Kinetic Roof Truss and Bogie Track Mechanism) and Business Component 104-B (Double-Skin Unitized ETFE/PV Hygrothermal and Acoustic Facade System). All aesthetic bowl layouts, seating sightlines, concourse retail spaces, standard structural foundations, and code-compliant MEP distribution systems are severed and excluded from the R&D claim at inception, eliminating any contamination from the I.R.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) style, taste, and cosmetic exclusion or routine engineering exclusions.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Technological Uncertainty and Process of Experimentation

Apex institutes a contemporaneous "Technical Experimentation Log" within its engineering document management system for Components 104-A and 104-B to satisfy I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A)–(C). Prior to schematic design, the lead structural engineer and facade physicist author a signed baseline uncertainty memorandum documenting why standard AISC steel design manuals and ASHRAE thermal standards cannot resolve the design of Components 104-A and 104-B—specifically demonstrating that thermal bridging across the kinetic roof seal and nonlinear seismic racking across a 720-foot asymmetrical span create coupled structural and hygrothermal uncertainties regarding appropriate design. Thereafter, every parametric model run, finite element analysis (FEA) iteration, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) thermal simulation, and boundary-layer wind-tunnel test is logged sequentially with a versioned hypothesis, test result, and failure analysis. For example, the log records that Iteration 104-A-v1 (dual-arch box truss with elastomeric bearings) failed the lateral drift threshold at due to torsional coupling; Iteration 104-A-v2 (tri-chord spatial truss with friction-pendulum isolators) reduced lateral drift by but exceeded bogie wheel load limits; and Iteration 104-A-v3 (hybrid cable-stayed spatial truss with articulated bogie equalizer beams) satisfied all deflection and seismic criteria. All superseded detail revisions, failed model outputs, and physical mock-up laboratory test reports are archived in a dedicated audit repository.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Time and QRE Accounting Governance

To satisfy I.R.C. § 6001 and the 80 percent "substantially all" threshold enforced in Little Sandy Coal, Apex configures its enterprise accounting system to require daily employee time entry into granular task codes under Components 104-A and 104-B, strictly segregating qualified experimental activities from excluded production work.

body.text: Because all routine production drafting, permitting, and foreign support hours are segregated outside Business Components 104-A and 104-B, Apex can mathematically prove that over 85 percent of the total hours applied to each discrete component constituted elements of a process of experimentation, fully satisfying the Seventh Circuit's standard in Little Sandy Coal and the Tax Court's substantiation requirements in Phoenix Design Group.
Case Study 2: Custom Industrial Environmental Remediation and Air Pollution Control System Design-Build Contract
Baseline Project Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Catalytic Environmental Systems, LLC ("CES"), an industrial chemical and mechanical engineering firm based in the United States, is contracted by a specialty semiconductor wafer manufacturer ("Client") to design, engineer, and build a first-of-its-kind Regenerative Thermal Oxidizer (RTO) and wet-scrubber abatement system capable of simultaneously destroying per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and pyrophoric silane off-gases from a high-velocity exhaust stream.

Under its unamended commercial workflow, CES enters into a Time-and-Materials Not-to-Exceed (T&M NTE) contract capped at $6,200,000, governed by the Client's standard Procurement Terms and Conditions. This baseline arrangement suffers from four fatal legal and evidentiary defects identified in Populous Holdings, Geosyntec, Betz, Smith, and LAFA 20223401F. First, under the T&M NTE structure, the Client reimburses CES bi-weekly for every engineering hour worked at scheduled billing rates up to $6.2 million regardless of whether the abatement system achieves target destruction efficiency; as established in Geosyntec and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and (3), hourly reimbursement guaranteed regardless of technical outcome is funded research at least to the extent of all client payments received. Second, the Client's procurement boilerplate states that all engineering designs, process flow diagrams (PFDs), piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs), catalyst formulations, and operating parameters developed under the contract constitute "Client Confidential Work-for-Hire," granting the Client exclusive rights to use the technology and barring CES from utilizing the abatement process design for any other customer. Under Lockheed Martin, Populous Holdings, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), this exclusivity and non-use restriction strips CES of substantial rights, rendering the entire project 100 percent funded even if CES incurs costs exceeding the $6.2 million cap. Third, CES purchases $1,400,000 in specialized Hastelloy C-276 reactor vessels, ceramic heat-exchange media, and analytical mass-spectrometry sensors, booking all material costs into a single general ledger construction account without distinguishing experimental pilot-unit supplies (§ 41(b)(2)(C)) from depreciable commercial equipment or post-commercial-production construction (§ 41(d)(4)(A)). Fourth, CES hires a third-party computational fluid dynamics (CFD) consultant for $350,000 on a lump-sum basis where the consultant is paid only upon delivering validated simulation results, yet CES attempts to claim 65 percent of the consultant's fee as a contract research expense under I.R.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) despite not bearing the financial risk of the subcontractor's work.
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring of Fee Mechanism, Acceptance Remedies, and IP Rights

Prior to executing the engagement, CES's tax counsel restructures the commercial agreement into a fixed-price, performance-contingent turnkey contract that satisfies the strict parameters of Populous Holdings, Fairchild, and Lockheed Martin. CES eliminates hourly T&M billing and converts the agreement into a strict Fixed-Price Lump-Sum contract ($6,200,000) divided into line-item technical deliverables, under which all milestone payments prior to final commissioning are legally designated as unearned provisional advances subject to final performance acceptance testing. The contract incorporates an explicit "Technical Performance Guarantee Schedule" requiring that, upon continuous 72-hour commissioning source testing, the integrated abatement unit must achieve at least Destruction and Removal Efficiency (DRE) for target PFAS compounds without generating dioxin or furan byproducts above , zero auto-ignition particulate fouling of the ceramic heat-recovery bed from pyrophoric silane, and total system pressure drop at a flow rate.

To satisfy the appellate standard of Fairchild, Grigsby, and MBJ, the default and warranty clauses explicitly stipulate that if the system fails to meet any metric in the Technical Performance Guarantee Schedule during source testing, the Client has the unconditional right to reject the system, withhold final payment, require CES to re-engineer, rebuild, and replace reactor internals entirely at CES's own cost without additional compensation, and—if CES fails to achieve compliance within 90 days—demand a 100 percent refund of all prior provisional advances alongside system removal at CES's expense. Simultaneously, the intellectual property clause is rewritten to satisfy the requirements of Judge Goeke's Populous and Lockheed Martin substantial rights test. While CES agrees not to disclose the Client's proprietary wafer-etching chemical recipes, the contract explicitly establishes that the Client's right to operate the physical RTO and scrubber unit at its facility is non-exclusive, that CES is not restricted in any manner from using the underlying thermodynamic research, reactor geometry, catalyst configurations, CFD models, and abatement process methodologies on future projects for any customer, and that CES shall never be required to pay a royalty, license fee, or other consideration to the Client to commercialize or reuse the research results in CES's ongoing business. Finally, to ensure that CES (rather than its third-party CFD consultant) can validly claim 65 percent of the subcontractor's costs as contract research expenses under I.R.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), CES restructures the subcontract onto a time-and-materials (non-contingent) basis where CES bears the financial risk of the subcontractor's research failure and retains all substantial rights in the subcontractor's CFD outputs.
Step 2: Sub-Component Definition and Pilot-Model Isolation

Rather than claiming the entire $6.2 million engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) project—which includes routine structural steel erection, concrete foundation pads, standard ductwork, and commercial off-the-shelf exhaust fans—CES defines two specific qualifying business components under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Specifically, CES isolates Business Component 201-A (Process/Technique), encompassing the High-Velocity Dual-Stage Pyrophoric Silane Oxidation and Fluorinated Gas Thermal Destruction Process, and Business Component 201-B (Pilot Model/Product), encompassing the Custom Hastelloy Venturi Quench and Acid-Gas Packed-Bed Scrubber Assembly evaluated under the pilot-model rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii).
Step 3: Structured Process of Experimentation and Iterative Testing Documentation

To satisfy the scientific method requirements enforced in Phoenix Design Group and Betz, CES's process engineers maintain a contemporaneous "R&D Design History File" (DHF) documenting both the baseline chemical kinetics uncertainty and the multi-alternative experimental process. The baseline engineering dossier establishes that standard RTO operating temperatures () fail to cleave carbon-fluorine bonds in PFAS, whereas elevating chamber temperatures to induces rapid silicon dioxide () glassification and plugging of standard ceramic media while generating corrosive hydrofluoric acid () vapor that attacks standard alloys. The DHF then systematically records four distinct chamber geometry and reagent-injection alternatives modeled via reactive-flow CFD and empirically tested in a 500 SCFM slip-stream pilot reactor prior to full-scale fabrication.

body.text: Step 4: Granular QRE Accounting for Wages, Direct Supervision/Support, and Supplies

CES implements strict accounting controls under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2) and § 6001 to ensure audit-ready substantiation. Engineers and technicians log hours daily against specific experimental work orders (WO-201A-EXP and WO-201B-PILOT), while routine commercial fabrication, site erection, OSHA safety meetings, procurement administration, and post-acceptance commercial production activities (§ 41(d)(4)(A)) are tracked to separate construction work orders (WO-201-CONST) that are completely excluded from the R&D claim. This segregation ensures that over 90 percent of the hours within the claimed business components represent direct experimentation, first-line supervision, or direct experimental test support under Little Sandy Coal. Concurrently, consumable reagents, sacrificial ceramic test media, corrosion coupons, and slip-stream pilot-unit fabrication materials consumed during the experimental trials are booked to a dedicated "R&D Experimental Supplies" general ledger account linked directly to WO-201A-EXP and WO-201B-PILOT under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C), whereas materials incorporated into the final commercial abatement unit qualify only to the extent the unit itself is substantiated as an uncertain pilot model under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii).
Strategic Synthesis for Tax Counsel and Technical Advisors

The U.S. Tax Court's December 6, 2019 Order in Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner remains an essential analytical milestone demonstrating that architectural, engineering, and technical service firms operating under fixed-price contracts are not categorically barred from claiming the federal R&D tax credit under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), even when clients retain ownership of physical design deliverables and architectural copyrights. Specifically, Judge Goeke's application of Lockheed Martin provides an enduring defensive framework for the "substantial rights" prong: so long as the contract does not prohibit the researcher from reusing the underlying technical concepts, engineering methodologies, and research results on future projects, and does not require the researcher to pay a royalty or license fee to the client for such reuse, the transfer of physical drawings or exterior aesthetic copyrights does not strip the taxpayer of substantial rights.

However, tax attorneys and technical advisors must never treat Populous Holdings as a blanket safe harbor for standard commercial fixed-price agreements. Because Populous Holdings was issued as a nonprecedential Rule 50(f) order, and because the Fifth and Eighth Circuits in United States v. Grigsby (2023) and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner (2024)—alongside the Tax Court in Smith v. Commissioner (2026)—have subsequently ruled that fixed-price contracts governed by general professional "standards of care" fail the payment-contingency requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), taxpayers relying on unmodified AIA or commercial service templates face severe audit exposure. To sustain an R&D tax credit claim under contemporary federal examination and judicial scrutiny, taxpayers must proactively integrate explicit quantitative technical acceptance criteria, non-conforming work rejection clauses, cure-at-own-expense and refund/clawback obligations, and unambiguous reservations of non-exclusive rights to underlying technical know-how directly into their client contracts, while simultaneously maintaining sub-component shrinking-back accounting and contemporaneous experimental documentation that satisfy the substantive rigors of Phoenix Design Group and Little Sandy Coal.

metaDescription: Populous Holdings v. Commissioner (2019): an architectural firm's research under fixed-price contracts was not funded because it bore the risk of failure.
